extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; aspiring critics and novelists studying novel form
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for judging or composing novels, especially the 'prophetic' aspect and the formal qualities called pattern and rhythm; illustrated with examples (Melville, Dostoevsky, Lawrence, Brontë, James, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet-as-novelist: uncanny advantages and intermittent realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarded as a novelist the prophet has certain uncanny advantages: he 'manipulates a beam of light' which occasionally touches domestic objects and renders them more vivid; prophetic fiction shows intermittent realism that can both smash or illumine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow prophetic passages into otherwise domestic scenes — the prophet may 'smash or distort' surroundings but can make ordinary things more vivid. This intermittent realism pervades works like Dostoevsky and Melville and is characterized by sudden, intense attention to small details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roughness of surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic works often display a 'roughness of surface' — while passing under our eyes they are 'full of dents and grooves and lumps and spikes' which provoke approval or disapproval; after the experience they become 'as smooth as the moon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the incidental roughness (unevenness, abruptness, jaggedness) as part of the prophetic effect; do not mistake it for defective workmanship — its roughness contributes to the work's vitality even if later memory recalls a smoother unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and suspension of humour required from reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction 'demands humility and the absence of the sense of humour' — readers must sometimes suspend their inclination to snigger or apply a single critical vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach prophetic works with humility: humour, incredulity, or mocking response will cause the prophetic 'treasure' to disappear. The reader may need to 'lay aside the single vision' usually brought to literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy's orientation toward unity and songlike expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy's 'face is towards unity' and it 'gives us the sensation of a song or of sound.' Unlike fantasy (whose confusion is fundamental), prophecy's confusion is incidental — the prophetic voice tends to sing rather than to 'talk'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize passages that function as an overarching song or undercurrent rather than as episodic fantasy; value unity and musicality of tone as hallmarks of prophetic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet's compositional stance: remoteness, non-reflection, and avoidance of hammering
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophet is imagined to be in a 'remoter emotional state' while composing: he 'does not reflect' and 'does not hammer away.' Authors who reflect, hammer or seek tools deliberately (Joyce, in the lecture's view) are excluded from pure prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author maintains an inward, trance-like velocity and avoids overt argumentation, over-explanation, or methodical 'tool-using' that turns song into talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreground detail used to reach universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic writers often sit with 'little things in the foreground' (small objects, precise factual detail) and through scrupulous, sometimes childlike attention make them gateways to larger effects — e.g., Dostoevsky's accurate trial descriptions, Melville's cataloguing of whale products, D.H. Lawrence's descriptive passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value carefully observed, occasionally encyclopedic detail as a means of evoking the universal and the prophetic song — the 'plain things' can become 'the knottiest' and most revealing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning as song or undercurrent rather than explicit symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic fiction (Moby Dick is the example) the essential meaning often 'flows athwart the action and the surface morality like an undercurrent' and lies outside words; turning incidental objects (the Delight, the coffin) into deliberate symbols 'silences the book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reductive symbolic readings that pin down the prophetic music into simple allegory; prefer interpretations that respect ambiguity and the musical/contestual nature of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of evil in prophetic fiction: transcendent and non-sordid
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil in prophetic works is not merely social or sexual misconduct nor a convenient plot device; it is often envisaged as a transcendent force (Melville's White Whale) or as a non-sordid, almost 'natural depravity' (Claggart in Billy Budd), which serves as a counterforce to the prophetic song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for representations of evil that are grand, ambiguous, or elemental rather than petty or merely villainous; such conception of evil often fuels the prophetic contest and reveals the writer's moral imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern as an aesthetic aspect: the book seen as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern is a formal/aesthetic quality causing us 'to see the book as a whole' — a pictorial or geometrical shape (hour-glass, grand chain) that gives pleasure beyond curiosity (story) or intelligence (plot). Pattern draws most nourishment from the plot but may be nourished by any element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, consider the global shape of the work (convergences, symmetries, cycles) and how that shape yields an aesthetic pleasure distinct from mere narrative interest. Examples: Thais (hour-glass), Roman Pictures (grand chain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of pattern to author's mood and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern is valuable when it matches the author's mood and the book's atmosphere (Roman Pictures): the pattern must be appropriate and seems to 'externalize' the atmosphere so that the closing action is the thing the book required from the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the chosen structural pattern organically fits the author's tone and ambience; mismatched or artificially imposed patterns will feel contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern often derives mainly from plot and may require authorial sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern 'springs mainly from the plot' and in tightly patterned books (e.g., Henry James's The Ambassadors) 'everything is planned, everything fits' — minor characters elaborate the main theme, and the author may sacrifice other freedoms to achieve the pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of planning, symmetry and the extent to which characters and incidents are harnessed to realize a unified shape; recognize that the triumph of pattern can involve deliberate restrictions on digression or looseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern vs. rhythm distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all beauty is pattern (shape as whole); when it is not the shape of the book we should call it 'rhythm.' The lecture borrows 'pattern' from painting and 'rhythm' from music and notes that both terms are vague in literary use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between static/architectural unity (pattern) and dynamic, recurring tempo or flow (rhythm) when analyzing a novel's aesthetic; expect 'rhythm' to be a less rigid, more musical quality that governs the book's movement rather than its overall shape.
